name: The No-Miracles Argument
statement: Science works so well it would be a miracle if its theories were not roughly true.
statementAccent: a miracle if its theories were not roughly true
meaning: The no-miracles argument, also called the miracle argument or the ultimate argument for scientific realism, is the leading argument in favor of realism about science. It holds that the predictive and practical success of mature scientific theories would be a miracle, an inexplicable coincidence, if those theories were not at least approximately true and their central theoretical terms did not genuinely refer to real, often unobservable, entities. Because the success of science is manifest, and only its approximate truth could explain that success, the argument concludes that we should believe our best theories to be approximately true, that is, we should be scientific realists. The argument is an inference to the best explanation applied at the level of science as a whole, a meta-level abduction: realism is put forward as the best, indeed the only non-miraculous, explanation of why science works. It is especially associated with Hilary Putnam, who put it in its famous form by saying that realism is the only philosophy that does not make the success of science a miracle, and with J. J. C. Smart, who gave an earlier version framed in terms of a cosmic coincidence. Richard Boyd developed a more sophisticated form grounding the reliability of scientific method in the approximate truth of background theories. The argument's key premise, that success indicates truth, is the target of the pessimistic induction.
mechanism: The no-miracles argument reasons from the success of science to the approximate truth of its theories by way of an inference to the best explanation. Its starting point is an undeniable fact: mature scientific theories are strikingly successful, making novel and precise predictions that come true and supporting reliable technologies that manipulate the world. The argument then asks what best explains this success. The realist answer is that the theories are at least approximately true and their central terms latch onto real features of the world; a true or nearly true theory would naturally yield accurate predictions and effective interventions, so its success is exactly what we should expect. The anti-realist, by contrast, must regard the sustained, novel success of theories about unobservables as a lucky coincidence, a miracle, since on the anti-realist view there is no reason connected with truth for the theories to work. Since a hypothesis that renders the evidence expected is a better explanation than one that leaves it a coincidence, the argument concludes that approximate truth is the best explanation of success, and infers realism. Smart's earlier version made the same point by charging the instrumentalist with believing in a cosmic coincidence, that the phenomena just happen to fall out as if the unobservable entities were real. Boyd sharpened the argument by noting that scientific methods are themselves theory-dependent, and that their reliability in producing successful predictions is best explained by the approximate truth of the background theories that inform them, turning the argument into an explanation of the success of scientific method as a whole.

examples.text: Putnam argued that realism is the only philosophy that does not make the success of science a miracle.
Smart charged that without realism, the success of theories about unobservables would be an odd cosmic coincidence.
The argument infers the approximate truth of theories as the best explanation of the success of science as a whole.

whyItMatters: The no-miracles argument is the central argument for scientific realism and one of the most discussed arguments in the philosophy of science. It gives sharp expression to a powerful and widely shared intuition, that the extraordinary success of science in predicting and controlling the world would be baffling, even miraculous, unless science were getting the world approximately right, an intuition that captures why so many scientists and laypeople take our best theories to describe reality, including its unobservable depths. Because the argument is an inference to the best explanation applied to science itself, it also ties the realism debate to deep questions about explanation, confirmation, and the legitimacy of abductive reasoning. Its prominence has made it the focus of the most important objections to realism: the pessimistic induction attacks its key premise by noting that past successful theories were often false, and critics have charged it with committing the base-rate fallacy or with begging the question by using the very abductive reasoning that anti-realists doubt. The debate it has generated, including van Fraassen's alternative Darwinian explanation of success, has clarified what the success of science can and cannot show.

working.text: take as given the striking predictive and practical success of mature scientific theories.
argue that only the approximate truth of the theories, not coincidence, can explain their success.
conclude, by inference to the best explanation, that our best theories are approximately true and their entities real.

limits: The no-miracles argument faces powerful objections aimed at each of its moves. The pessimistic induction attacks its central premise: the history of science shows many theories that were empirically successful yet later judged false, with non-referring central terms, such as those positing caloric, phlogiston, and the ether, so success does not reliably indicate truth, and the realist's inference is undermined by science's own track record. A second objection, pressed by Colin Howson and by P. D. Magnus and Craig Callender, is that the argument commits the base-rate fallacy: inferring probable truth from success while ignoring the prior probability, or base rate, of true theories renders the probabilistic reasoning fallacious. A third objection, associated with van Fraassen and Arthur Fine, is that the argument begs the question against the anti-realist, since it defends realism by an inference to the best explanation, and abduction is exactly the mode of reasoning the anti-realist doubts, so the argument assumes what it needs to prove. Van Fraassen also offers an alternative, Darwinian explanation of success: successful theories survive because unsuccessful ones are discarded, so success needs no realist explanation. Not all realists even require genuine reference of theoretical terms, and the exact wording of Putnam's formulation should be handled with care.
misreadings: The no-miracles argument is not a proof that our theories are true, but a fallible inference to the best explanation that they are approximately true. It does not claim that anti-realists deny the success of science, only that they cannot explain it without treating it as a coincidence. And it is not immune to its own abductive character, since critics charge that using inference to the best explanation to defend realism begs the question against those who doubt such inference, so treating the argument as a proof, as denying scientific success to anti-realists, or as beyond the reach of its own method, misreads it.
origin: The central argument for scientific realism, associated with Hilary Putnam and J. J. C. Smart, that the success of science would be a miracle unless its theories were approximately true, cast as an inference to the best explanation and challenged by the pessimistic induction.
